paragraphs.heading: What the word means
paragraphs.text: Eutrophication is the buildup of nutrients in a body of water, which drives extra growth of living things that can use up the water's oxygen. The word comes from the Greek eutrophos, meaning well-nourished. It can happen on its own or because of people. When people cause it, by releasing sewage, industrial wastewater, fertilizer runoff and other nutrient sources, it is called cultural eutrophication.

paragraphs.heading: Poor, middling and rich waters
paragraphs.text: Water bodies get different names depending on how many nutrients they hold. Water with very few nutrients is called oligotrophic, and water with a moderate amount is called mesotrophic. Very advanced eutrophication may be described as dystrophic or hypertrophic. One definition sums the whole thing up as water quality getting worse because added nutrients cause too much plant growth, mostly algae, followed by decay.

paragraphs.heading: What goes wrong
paragraphs.text: Extra phosphorus and nitrogen let some water plants, especially algae, grow fast and bloom in dense numbers. These blooms can shade out plants living on the bottom, changing the whole plant community. When the algae die, bacteria break them down and remove oxygen, which can leave the water anoxic, meaning without oxygen. That kills animals that need oxygen, such as fish and invertebrates. Over time, favouring species that thrive on rich nutrients can disrupt whole food webs and cut the variety of species.

paragraphs.heading: Which nutrient matters
paragraphs.text: Which nutrient holds back growth differs from place to place. In most freshwater ecosystems, phosphorus is the factor that limits plant growth, while in the sea, nitrogen is the main limiting nutrient. The main sources of nitrogen pollution are farm runoff carrying fertilizers and animal waste, sewage, and nitrogen settling out of the air from burning or animal waste. Nitrous oxide from burning fossil fuels has raised nitrogen levels in the ocean and made eutrophication there worse.

paragraphs.heading: The lake split in two
paragraphs.text: Eutrophication was recognised as a pollution problem in lakes and reservoirs of Europe and North America in the mid-20th century. In the 1970s, research at the Experimental Lakes Area in Ontario, Canada, showed that fresh waters are limited by phosphorus. In 1973, researchers divided Lake 226 into two basins with a curtain that water could not pass through. Both halves got nitrogen and carbon, but only one got phosphorus. Only that half grew a large algal bloom.

paragraphs.heading: Sources and fixes
paragraphs.text: Detergents containing phosphate added to the problem until they were phased out in the 1970s, and since then sewage and farming have become the main phosphate sources. Shallow waters are the most vulnerable. On shorelines and in shallow lakes, wind and waves often stir up sediment, which can release nutrients into the water and make eutrophication worse. Ways to prevent or reverse it include cutting pollution from sewage and farms, and adding shellfish and seaweed can help reduce nitrogen pollution.
